title: How to Use AI to Save Time Without Losing Yourself
guestBio: Nicole McCain is the Chief AI Officer and Founder of Gentiv-AI Solutions, a corporate AI trainer, speaker, and future-of-work strategist who has trained 5,200+ business owners and team members. With 20+ years leading Fortune 500 technology initiatives, she helps women-led businesses adopt AI without chaos, wasted spend, or losing the human touch. She is the author of The AI-Powered One Hour Workday and a board member of the National Association of Women in AI.
excerpt: Nicole McCain, author of The AI-Powered One Hour Workday, joins Aimee to break down why layering AI on top of a messy, overloaded life only multiplies the chaos. She shares her H.A.S. framework and the one audit every woman should run before she automates a single thing.
metaDescription: Nicole McCain teaches women how to audit before they automate — so AI saves time without replacing the human parts that matter most.
keyTakeaways: Laying AI on top of a messy, overwhelming workflow doesn't create freedom — it multiplies the chaos you already have.
The right order is eliminate, simplify, and delegate before you ever consider automating anything.
Nicole's H.A.S. framework — Human, Automate, Support — gives you a clear filter for deciding what AI gets and what stays yours.
Your lived experience, your judgment, and your relationships are not efficiency problems to solve; they are the irreplaceable human layer that AI should never touch.
Use AI for the draft, but always bring your own voice, story, and perspective to the final version — that's what readers actually connect with.
Before any AI tool touches your work or family life, read the privacy policy, turn off model training on your data, and keep your children's real names out of the tools.
If AI gives you time back, the most powerful question you can ask is not 'what can I produce now?' but 'what do I actually want to do with this life?'

quiz.title: What's Your AI Personality Type?
quiz.description: You know AI is supposed to make your life easier — but somewhere between the hype and the hustle, something got lost. This quiz helps you figure out exactly where you are with AI right now, and what kind of support will actually move the needle for you.

A.name: The Reluctant Skeptic
A.description: You're smart, capable, and deeply suspicious of anything that promises to do your thinking for you — and honestly, that instinct has served you well. You've watched enough trends come and go to know that not every shiny tool deserves a spot in your workflow. What you might be missing, though, is the specific framework that separates AI as a crutch from AI as a genuinely useful filter for your already-excellent judgment. This episode was made for you — Nicole McCain speaks your language, and her audit-first approach will feel like a relief, not a sales pitch.

B.name: The Eager Automator
B.description: You are all in. You've downloaded the apps, built the workflows, and told at least three people they need to try this — and you mean it. Your enthusiasm is a genuine asset, but if you're honest, the overwhelm hasn't quite gone away the way you expected it to. Nicole's episode is your recalibration moment: it will help you slow down long enough to make sure what you're automating is actually worth keeping in the first place.

C.name: The Invisible Load Carrier
C.description: Your plate isn't just full — it has plates stacked on top of it. You run the household logic, the emotional temperature of your team, the schedule that nobody else can decode, and somehow you're also supposed to now learn AI. The idea of adding one more tool feels laughable. What you need first isn't an AI tutorial; it's the permission to audit what's already there — and Nicole McCain's conversation with Aimee gives you exactly that framework, in plain language, without judgment.

D.name: The Intentional Builder
D.description: You think before you adopt. You ask 'what problem am I actually solving?' before you invest time in any new system — and that discipline is rare and valuable. You're not anti-AI; you're anti-chaos. Nicole's H.A.S. framework and her audit-first philosophy will feel like a natural extension of how you already think, and this episode will give you the language to bring the people around you along with you.

questions.question: It's Monday morning and someone tells you a new AI tool will save you five hours a week. Your first thought is:

options.text: Interesting — but what's the catch, and who benefits from me believing that?
Where do I sign up? Five hours is five hours.
I don't even have five hours to learn the tool.
Maybe — but first I want to know exactly which five hours and what I'd do with them.

questions.question: When you think about the invisible work in your life — the logistics no one sees — you mostly feel:

options.text: Skeptical that any tool could actually understand the complexity of it.
Excited, because automation is exactly what this kind of work is made for.
Exhausted just thinking about it — it's a lot, and it's mostly invisible to everyone else.
Ready to map it out, categorize it, and decide what actually needs to change.

questions.question: You've been asked to write a piece of content for your business. You decide to use AI to help. How do you actually use it?

options.text: I ask it for ideas but rewrite everything from scratch — I don't want my voice to disappear.
I let it draft the whole thing and do a quick pass to clean it up.
I mean to use it, but by the time I get there, I'm too tired and just write it myself.
I use it for the structure and research, then rewrite the core message in my own words.

questions.question: Someone mentions AI safety and kids in the same sentence. You:

options.text: Have questions, but you're not sure who to trust for unbiased information on it.
Figure the platforms handle that — you trust the terms of service.
Feel a wave of anxiety because your kids are already online and you haven't thought about this enough.
Already have opinions about this and have started having conversations with your family about it.

questions.question: If AI genuinely gave you back ten hours a week, your honest first instinct would be to:

options.text: Wonder what the real cost is — nothing is actually free.
Fill it with more projects. More output means more progress.
Sleep. Rest. Breathe. Maybe finally do the thing you've been saying you'd do for two years.
Sit down and decide intentionally how to use it before anything else fills it back up.

questions.question: When it comes to your relationship with productivity, the statement that feels most true right now is:

options.text: I'm productive, but I'm not sure all of it is pointed in the right direction.
I measure my worth by how much I get done — and AI is a tool to get more done.
I'm running as fast as I can and I still feel behind. Productive is not how I'd describe it.
I've started to question whether 'more productive' is even the right goal anymore.

content:
You've downloaded the apps. You've watched the tutorials. You've been told — more times than you can count — that AI is going to give you your time back. And yet, if you're being honest, you feel more overwhelmed than you did before you started. You're not imagining it. And you are not the problem.

In Episode 77 of The Manage Her® Podcast, host Aimee Rickabus sits down with Nicole McCain — Chief AI Officer, founder of Gentiv-AI Solutions, corporate AI trainer, and author of The AI-Powered One Hour Workday — for one of the most grounded, practical, and permission-giving conversations the show has ever aired. Nicole has trained 5,200+ business owners and team members. She spent 20+ years in Fortune 500 technology. And she's also a mom who has had to figure out what AI means not just for her business, but for her kitchen, her schedule, and her daughters' lives.

The Coaching Moment That Changed Everything

Nicole's turning point didn't come from a productivity hack. It came from a coach who looked at her packed calendar and said, plainly, "You are not important." Not as a verdict — as a diagnosis. Because Nicole had built a life where the answer to every demand was yes, where her name appeared on every task, and where being needed had quietly become the whole identity. Sound familiar? That one question cracked open an audit she didn't know she needed to run — not of her AI tools, but of her actual life.

That moment is the foundation of everything Nicole teaches. Before you automate a single thing, you have to see the full picture of what you're actually doing. The invisible work. The emotional labor. The tasks that exist only because no one ever questioned them. You cannot delegate your way out of chaos that you haven't named yet.

Audit Before You Automate

Nicole's first rule — the one she gives every single client before they open a single AI tool — is this: audit before you automate. Most women arrive at AI tools carrying years of accumulated workflow weight. Half of what's on their plates shouldn't be automated. It should be eliminated. The order she prescribes is deliberate and non-negotiable: eliminate first, simplify second, delegate third, automate last. Skipping to automation before doing that work doesn't save you time. It just runs your chaos faster.

This is where Nicole's conversation with Aimee gets especially real. Because "doing more" has been sold to women as the goal for so long that we've forgotten to ask whether the things we're doing deserve to be done at all — let alone done by a machine.

The H.A.S. Framework: Human, Automate, Support

Once you've audited what's actually on your plate, Nicole introduces the filter she uses in her business, her home, and her coaching: the H.A.S. framework — Human, Automate, Support.

Human is the category that doesn't move. Your judgment. Your care. Your relationships. The moments where a person needs to feel a person on the other end. These are not efficiency problems. They are the whole point. Nicole is adamant: before you decide what AI gets, you decide what stays yours.

Automate covers the repeatable, rules-based, low-stakes tasks — scheduling, formatting, data sorting, first drafts of content that you will always revise. These are the tasks that drain your energy without requiring your intelligence, and they're fair game.

Support sits in the middle — tasks where AI can assist, inform, or accelerate you, but where your discernment has to remain in the loop. Research is a good example. AI can pull it together; you have to evaluate it.

Nicole uses this framework in her household the same way she uses it in her business. The question is never just "can AI do this?" It's "should AI do this, and what do I lose if it does?"

The 90/10 Rule and the Morning Brief

One of the most practical sections of this episode is Nicole walking through her actual morning routine. She starts each day with what she calls a chief of staff brief — a structured AI-assisted summary of her priorities, her calendar, and anything she needs to make decisions about before she opens her inbox. It takes minutes. It replaces the mental scramble that used to eat the first hour of her day.

But she's equally clear about where the handoff ends. The 90/10 rule: AI can generate up to 90% of a draft — structure, data, outline, even language — but the final 10% is always hers. The story only she can tell. The opinion that comes from having lived something. The voice that her audience actually follows. That 10% is not a small finishing touch. It's the whole reason the content works.

AI Safety at Home Is Not Optional

If you are a parent, do not skip the second half of this episode. Nicole shares the moment she discovered an AI chat app on her daughter's school-issued laptop — and what it revealed about how little most of us understand about where our children's conversations are going and who's training on them.

She doesn't panic. She educates. But she is fierce about it. Read the privacy policy. Turn off model training on your personal data. Keep your children's real names, schools, and routines out of AI tools. These are not hypothetical risks. They are current ones, and the women who understand them now will be the ones raising kids who know how to navigate this world with both capability and caution.

What Do You Actually Want?

The question Aimee and Nicole close on is the one this whole episode has been building toward. If AI genuinely gives you time back — and used correctly, it will — what are you going to do with it? Not produce more. Not optimize harder. What do you actually want? For most women who've spent years being everything to everyone, that question is harder to answer than any productivity framework. But it's the only one worth starting with.

This episode will not just teach you how to use AI better. It will ask you to get honest about why you wanted to save time in the first place — and whether the life you're building with that time is the one you actually chose.
